mcqs.q: Dental caries is best defined as a:
opts: Microbial disease of the calcified tissues of the teeth
Genetic disease of the jaw bone
mcqs.explain: Dental caries is a microbial disease of the calcified tissues of the teeth.

mcqs.q: Caries is characterised by:
opts: Demineralization of the inorganic portion and destruction of the organic substance
mcqs.explain: It involves demineralization of the inorganic portion and destruction of the organic substance of the tooth.

mcqs.q: The currently accepted theory of caries etiology is the:
mcqs.explain: The acidogenic theory is the accepted one — bacteria ferment carbohydrates to acids that demineralize the tooth.

mcqs.q: Keyes' triad for caries requires a susceptible host, a fermentable substrate and:
mcqs.explain: Keyes' triad = host/tooth + micro-organisms + substrate (diet), interacting over time.

mcqs.q: Which is a HOST factor in caries?
mcqs.explain: Host factors include the tooth (composition, morphology, position) and saliva (pH, quantity, viscosity, antibacterial factors).

mcqs.q: The dietary factor most important for caries is the:
mcqs.explain: The fermentable carbohydrate content of the diet provides the substrate that bacteria ferment to acid.

mcqs.q: The chief INITIATOR of dental caries is:
mcqs.explain: Streptococcus mutans is the chief initiator of caries; lactobacilli are linked to progression.

mcqs.q: Which organism is most associated with the PROGRESSION of a carious lesion?
mcqs.explain: Lactobacilli are associated with the progression of caries (S. mutans initiates it).

mcqs.q: Actinomyces is particularly implicated in:
mcqs.explain: Actinomyces is implicated in root-surface caries.

mcqs.q: Caries classified by morphology/site includes:
opts: Pit & fissure, smooth surface, and root caries
mcqs.explain: By morphology/site: pit & fissure caries, smooth surface caries and root caries.

mcqs.q: 'Nursing-bottle caries' is a classification based on:
mcqs.explain: Classification by age includes nursing-bottle caries (infants), adolescent caries and geriatric/senile caries.

mcqs.q: An early, REVERSIBLE carious lesion (white-spot) is termed:
mcqs.explain: Incipient/initial caries is the early, reversible lesion (white-spot).

mcqs.q: Caries that has STOPPED progressing and become hard and shiny is:
mcqs.explain: Arrested caries (eburnation) has stopped progressing.

mcqs.q: Caries occurring at the margin of an existing restoration is:
mcqs.explain: Recurrent (secondary) caries occurs at the margins of an existing restoration.

mcqs.q: Rapidly progressing caries affecting many teeth, including normally caries-resistant surfaces, is:
mcqs.explain: Rampant caries is rapidly progressing and widespread.

mcqs.q: Caries classified by SURFACES involved as simple, compound and complex refers to:
opts: 1 surface, 2 surfaces, and 3 or more surfaces
mcqs.explain: Simple = one surface, compound = two surfaces, complex = three or more surfaces.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised method of diagnosing caries?
opts: Visual, visual-tactile, dye penetration, radiographic, fibre-optic
mcqs.explain: Caries diagnosis: visual, visual & tactile, enhanced visual, dye penetration, radiographic and fibre-optic methods.

mcqs.q: Conventional, xeroradiography and digital imaging are subtypes of which diagnostic method?
mcqs.explain: Radiographic examination includes conventional, xeroradiography and digital imaging.

mcqs.q: Histologically, dentin caries is classically described in how many zones?
mcqs.explain: Dentin caries is described in five zones.

mcqs.q: The INNERMOST zone of dentin caries, with normal tubules and no bacteria, is:
mcqs.explain: Zone 1 (fatty degeneration) is the innermost layer — tubules appear normal with no crystals or bacteria.

mcqs.q: Deposition of fine crystals within the dentinal tubules at the advancing front is:
mcqs.explain: Zone 2 (dentinal sclerosis) shows fine crystal deposition within tubules at the advancing front.

mcqs.q: The transparent, demineralized, softer zone of dentin caries is:
mcqs.explain: Zone 3 (decalcification) is transparent and softer due to demineralization.

mcqs.q: The 'turbid dentin' zone with widened tubules packed with micro-organisms is:
mcqs.explain: Zone 4 (bacterial invasion) is the turbid dentin, with widened/distorted tubules packed with bacteria and collagen denaturation.

mcqs.q: Liquefaction foci of Miller and transverse clefts are features of:
mcqs.explain: Zone 5 (decomposed dentin), the outermost zone, shows liquefaction foci of Miller and transverse clefts.

mcqs.q: Mechanical oral-hygiene methods of caries prevention include:
mcqs.explain: Mechanical oral hygiene = brushing, flossing and prophylaxis; chemical = mouthwash, dentifrice and disclosing agents.

mcqs.q: Erythrosine is used in caries prevention as a:
mcqs.explain: Erythrosine is a disclosing agent used to reveal dental plaque (a chemical oral-hygiene aid).

mcqs.q: Which dietary changes are advised for caries prevention?
opts: Fibrous food, tea, cheese and milk (limit sugars)
mcqs.explain: Diet modification favours fibrous food, tea, cheese and milk, and limits fermentable sugars.

mcqs.q: Fluorides for caries prevention are delivered as:
mcqs.explain: Fluorides are delivered systemically and topically.

mcqs.q: Pit and fissure sealants prevent caries by:
opts: Physically sealing the deep grooves of posterior teeth
mcqs.explain: Pit and fissure sealants physically seal the susceptible deep grooves, preventing plaque accumulation.

mcqs.q: Untreated caries can spread, causing all of these sequelae EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: Sequelae of caries/spread of infection: cellulitis, tissue-space infection, Ludwig's angina, maxillary sinusitis and focal infection. Enamel hypoplasia is a developmental defect, not a sequela.

mcqs.q: 'Cellulitis' is best described as:
opts: Diffuse soft-tissue inflammation spreading through tissue spaces and fascial planes
mcqs.explain: Cellulitis is a diffuse, non-circumscribed inflammation of soft tissues that spreads through tissue spaces and along fascial planes.

mcqs.q: A life-threatening cellulitis beginning in the submandibular space is:
mcqs.explain: Ludwig's angina is an acute, potentially life-threatening toxic cellulitis beginning in the submandibular space and involving the sublingual and submental spaces.

mcqs.q: Acute/chronic inflammation of the maxillary sinus from direct spread of dental infection is:
mcqs.explain: Maxillary sinusitis is inflammation of the maxillary sinus, often from direct extension of a dental infection.

mcqs.q: A 'focal infection' is:
opts: A localized or general infection from dissemination of microorganisms/toxins from a focus
An infection limited to one tooth forever
mcqs.explain: A focal infection is a localized or general infection caused by dissemination of microorganisms or toxic products from a focus of infection.

mcqs.q: Tissue spaces are important in spread of infection because they are:
opts: Potential spaces between fascial planes forming pathways for infection
mcqs.explain: Tissue spaces are potential spaces between fascial planes that form natural pathways along which infection may spread.

mcqs.q: The enamel/dentin carious lesion classically advances in the shape of a:
mcqs.explain: Caries advances as a cone/triangle (the 'cones of caries'), differing between pit-and-fissure and smooth-surface lesions.

saqs.a: Dental caries is a microbial disease of the calcified tissues of the teeth, characterised by demineralization of the inorganic portion and destruction of the organic substance of the tooth.

saqs.q: State the components of Keyes' triad.
saqs.a: A susceptible host/tooth, cariogenic micro-organisms, and a fermentable substrate (diet) — interacting over time.

saqs.q: Name three cariogenic micro-organisms and their roles.
List the four ways of classifying dental caries.
saqs.a: By morphology/site (pit & fissure, smooth surface, root), by age (nursing-bottle, adolescent, geriatric), by severity/progress (incipient, rampant, arrested, recurrent), and by surfaces involved (simple, compound, complex).

saqs.q: List the five zones of dentin caries.
saqs.a: 1) Fatty degeneration, 2) Dentinal sclerosis, 3) Decalcification, 4) Bacterial invasion (turbid dentin), 5) Decomposed dentin (liquefaction foci of Miller).

saqs.q: List the methods of preventing dental caries.
saqs.a: Oral hygiene (mechanical & chemical), diet modification, fluorides (systemic & topical), pit & fissure sealants, salivary stimulants, and advanced methods (lasers, polymeric coatings).

saqs.q: List the sequelae of dental caries (spread of oral infection).
saqs.a: Cellulitis, spread through tissue spaces, Ludwig's angina, maxillary sinusitis, and focal infection.
